title: A Petri-net token is a resource
goal: Read places, transitions and markings, then trace one shared printer without inventing tokens.

sources.title: Original illustrative example
sources.location: Authored demo; not a real course, assessment or financial forecast.

cues.text: We have one printer. A token in Idle means that printer is available. No token in Busy means no job is currently using it.
Circles are places, which hold tokens. Bars are transitions, which describe events. Arrows say what each event consumes and produces.
Fire Start: consume the token from Idle and produce one in Busy. The same resource has changed state, rather than being duplicated.
Now the printer is busy. A second Start cannot fire because its input place, Idle, has no token.

steps.note: Start consumes Idle and produces Busy. Idle is now empty.

scenes.title: Trace a job, a release, and another job

cues.text: Begin again with one idle printer. Start the first job by moving the available resource from Idle to Busy.
While Busy has the resource, Idle is empty. Starting a second job is disabled; wanting to start it does not create a token.
Finish the first job. Consume Busy, return a token to Idle, and add one to Done to record a completed job.
Now Start can fire again. The printer becomes Busy while the completed job remains recorded in Done.
Count only the resource places, Idle and Busy. Their token counts always sum to one in this model.
Initially, one idle token plus zero busy tokens equals one printer. This matches our starting assumption.
During a job, zero idle tokens plus one busy token still equals one. Starting and finishing preserve the printer count.
Done is a separate count of completed jobs. Adding Done to that sum would mix resource availability with recorded history.

steps.note: M gives the token count in a place.
During a job: the same printer is in use.

scenes.title: Do not read more into a token

cues.text: A token does not automatically mean one second or one person. Its meaning comes from the model we chose.
Enabled means an event can fire, not that it must fire immediately. This untimed model does not tell us how long printing takes.
Check every output arc when an event fires. Finish both releases the printer and records completion; those outputs have different meanings.

steps.title: Meaning comes from the model
steps.body: Here Idle and Busy track one resource.

steps.title: Enabled is not inevitable
steps.body: No timing or scheduling policy is implied.

steps.title: Read every output arc
steps.body: Finish returns the printer and records a completed job.

scenes.title: The printer is busy: what can happen?

cues.text: Suppose Idle has zero tokens, Busy has one, and Done has zero. Which transition is enabled, and what happens if it fires?
Start is disabled because Idle is empty. Finish is enabled because Busy contains its required input token.
Fire Finish. Busy becomes empty, Idle becomes one, and Done becomes one. The resource is available again.
Check the resource invariant: Idle plus Busy is still one. We have recorded a completion without creating an extra printer.

check.question: Why can Start not fire while the printer is busy?
check.answer: Its input place Idle has no token. A transition is enabled only when all its required input tokens are available.

cues.text: First ask what each place and token means. This connects the drawing to the real resource or condition being modeled.
Next check whether every input token for a transition is present. Only then apply all the input and output changes together.
Finally interpret the new marking and check any invariant. That turns a moving diagram into an explanation you can verify.
